description: BioHacking Village at DEF CON 27 explores the intersection of security, biology, and DIY innovation. The 14 talks cover medical device security, biomedical engineering, DIY medicine, prosthetics, biohybrid materials, and the ethical implications of hacking biology.

talks.teaser: Medical misinformation has been labeled as one of the greatest public health threats of our time. Previously eradicated diseases, such as measles are occurring in clusters and causing deaths. The problem is complex wi...
talks.summary:
### Translating Cybersecurity Doctrines to Public Health
At 00:00, Dr. Eric Perakslis, Rubenstein Fellow at Duke University and former Chief Information Officer at the FDA, presents on applying cybersecurity methodologies to combat medical misinformation at the Biohacking Village.

### Field Realities of Epidemic Response
At 05:18, Dr. Perakslis shares firsthand experiences managing medical data systems during infectious disease outbreaks, including cholera, Ebola, and measles. He describes how public panic, infrastructure failures, and quarantine constraints complicate healthcare logistics.

### The Weaponization of Digital Health Misinformation
At 10:00, the speaker analyzes how malicious actors weaponize social media algorithms. Coordinated disinformation campaigns exploit algorithmic recommendation engines to promote unverified medical treatments and discourage vaccination, resulting in tangible public health harms.

### Threat Modeling Health Information Ecosystems
At 15:20, Dr. Perakslis demonstrates how to apply cybersecurity frameworks—such as threat modeling, attack surface analysis, and adversary motive profiling—to digital healthcare communication channels.

### Proactive Interventions and Defensive Red Teaming
Concluding between 20:28 and 27:12, Dr. Perakslis calls for cross-disciplinary collaboration between cybersecurity specialists, medical professionals, and behavioral scientists. He recommends deploying red-teaming exercises and information provenance verification to protect vulnerable populations from predatory health disinformation.

talks.title: The Attack Surface of a Networked Medical Device
talks.teaser: Even a device with the most ironclad firmware can still be subject to a broad variety of attacks depending on its interaction with other external components. This presentation will examine commonly overlooked vulnerab...
talks.summary:
### Networked Medical Devices and Clinical Threat Surfaces
At 00:00, Professor Avi Rubin (Johns Hopkins University) explores the attack surfaces and threat models associated with modern networked and implantable medical devices across hospital ecosystems.

### The Critical Imperative of Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)
At 07:03, Dr. Rubin explains the vital role of Software Bills of Materials (SBOMs) in healthcare. Medical devices—including infusion pumps, surgical robotics, and bedside monitors—regularly embed commercial off-the-shelf software components and legacy third-party libraries that harbor documented vulnerabilities.

### The Regulatory Patching Dilemma
At 14:01, the presentation examines the operational conflict between vulnerability remediation and regulatory compliance. Healthcare facilities often delay patching vulnerable devices due to fears of invalidating FDA 510(k) clearances or inadvertently causing clinical downtime in life-support equipment.

### Cloud Telemetry and Transport Security Risks
At 21:00, Dr. Rubin evaluates the push toward cloud-connected medical devices. He expresses skepticism regarding streaming sensitive patient physiological telemetry to external cloud platforms, discussing risks of unauthenticated access, HIPAA compliance violations, and network latency.

### Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) and Device Interfaces
Concluding between 28:00 and 35:00, the speaker details wireless attack vectors. Wearable and implantable devices frequently rely on Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) to communicate with patient smartphones, exposing pairing handshakes to eavesdropping and replay attacks. He concludes by praising recent FDA cybersecurity guidance and urging researchers to engage in responsible disclosure with medical manufacturers.

talks.title: Medical Simulations Panel
talks.summary:
### Clinical Implications of Hospital Cyber Disruptions
At 00:00, clinicians, simulation educators, and medical device security researchers convene at the Biohacking Village to explore how medical simulation centers can prepare healthcare systems for cyber attacks. The panel highlights that cybersecurity in healthcare directly affects patient morbidity and mortality.

### Real-World Impacts on Emergency Care and Triage
At 12:44, the panelists examine clinical failure modes during network outages and ransomware incidents. They discuss how disruptions to electronic health records (EHR) and telemetry networks blind emergency clinicians, delay critical medication delivery, and force hospitals to divert ambulances to neighboring facilities.

### Resource Constraints Among Device Manufacturers and Rural Clinics
At 26:11, the discussion addresses disparities across healthcare manufacturing. While major corporations maintain dedicated product security teams, smaller medical device vendors and rural healthcare clinics lack the engineering resources required to patch legacy equipment and remediate vulnerabilities quickly.

### Translating Cyber Vulnerabilities into Clinical Simulations
At 39:26, simulation educators demonstrate how hands-on training drills bridge the communication gap between IT security and medical staff. By simulating scenarios where compromised infusion pumps deliver incorrect dosages or monitors display corrupted vital signs, clinicians learn to recognize cyber disruptions during patient care.

### Cross-Disciplinary Incident Response Protocols
Concluding between 45:00 and 52:03, the panel advocates for integrated incident response playbooks. Panelists urge hospital leadership to embed clinical engineering, biomedical staff, and frontline medical providers into cybersecurity drills to ensure patient safety remains paramount during cyber incidents.

talks.teaser: Want to learn how an epic clash between hackers turns into a battle of survival? How an intense, immersive experience builds critical cybersecurity skills? This talk highlights how storytelling, gamification and theat...
talks.summary:
### Advancing Experiential Cybersecurity Learning
At 00:00, cybersecurity executive JC Vega delivers an energetic presentation on transforming technical training through realistic experiential learning and immersive crisis simulation exercises.

### Moving Beyond Static Syllabi to Mission-Driven Scenarios
At 06:02, Vega contrasts static classroom lectures with immersive simulation exercises. Effective operational training requires placing participants in realistic scenarios where they are provided with ambiguous objectives, incomplete data, and dynamic adversaries.

### Integrating Multi-Disciplinary Crisis Pressures
At 12:03, the speaker emphasizes that technical compromise is only one facet of a major cyber crisis. Realistic simulations must incorporate external pressures—including mock media interviews, public relations fallout, regulatory reporting deadlines, and legal liability constraints.

### The Pedagogical Value of Consequence
At 18:00, Vega argues that genuine learning occurs when operational decisions carry palpable consequences. Allowing teams to experience the failure of poor technical decisions under pressure instills visceral muscle memory that theoretical training cannot replicate.

### Multi-Agency Coordination and Supply Chain Dependencies
Concluding between 24:01 and 30:01, Vega highlights external organizational dependencies. Modern enterprise defense relies heavily on coordinating with external hosting providers, critical vendors, legal counsel, and law enforcement, emphasizing that incident response teams must practice cross-organizational collaboration before a real breach occurs.

talks.teaser: I will present two case studies of groups using biohacking methods to create generic versions of two of the most widely prescribed and most expensive pharmaceuticals in America. I will explain their methods and motiva...
talks.summary:
### The Ethics and Urgency of Open-Source Medicine
At 00:00, bioethicist Alex Pearlman examines the ethical, legal, and humanitarian motivations behind the DIY medicine and biohacking movements at the Biohacking Village. Pearlman discusses how skyrocketing healthcare costs drive patients toward grassroots alternatives.

### Economic Realities of Prescription Drug Pricing
At 08:59, Pearlman challenges pharmaceutical industry justifications for escalating drug costs. She critiques claims that exorbitant prices simply fund research and development, examining dramatic price hikes on off-patent, century-old essential medicines such as insulin and epinephrine.

### Guerrilla Pharma: Decentralized Chemistry and Open Formulations
At 17:50, the presentation explores activist collectives, highlighting projects like the Four Thieves Vinegar Collective. Pearlman analyzes automated mini-reactors and open-source chemical synthesis guides designed to allow individuals to manufacture critical medications outside commercial supply chains.

### Navigating Patient Autonomy and Clinical Risk
At 27:19, the speaker examines bioethical trade-offs. While acknowledging the grave safety risks associated with unregulated chemical synthesis—such as chemical toxicity, dosage errors, and absence of quality control—she argues that pricing patients out of life-saving medicine presents an immediate mortal threat that compels radical action.

### Demanding Systemic Pharmaceutical Reform
Concluding between 30:00 and 34:00, Pearlman emphasizes that DIY medicine represents a desperate symptom of systemic healthcare failure. She calls for comprehensive patent reform, increased public research funding, and international access initiatives to ensure life-saving pharmaceuticals remain universally accessible.

talks.title: Amputees and Prosthetics Challenges
talks.teaser: The human body is the most elegant and complex machine ever created, but often we do not realize how well it works until a major system has been compromised such as with an amputation severing and removing an element ...
talks.summary:
### Biomechanical and Technical Challenges in Prosthetics
At 00:00, biomedical engineer and certified prosthetist Wayne Penn presents a comprehensive exploration of the clinical, mechanical, and electronic engineering challenges in modern artificial limb design.

### Anatomical Socket Casting and High-Fidelity Imaging
At 13:03, Penn explains the foundational challenge of prosthetic design: the interface between the residual limb and the artificial socket. He demonstrates plaster casting and trans-femoral imaging, illustrating how micro-shifts in weight distribution cause tissue necrosis, skin abrasions, and extreme discomfort.

### Global Amputation Demographics and Etiology
At 26:01, the speaker dispels common misconceptions regarding the causes of limb loss. While public perception often focuses on military combat injuries and acute trauma, vascular disease and diabetes account for over 80% of amputations globally, demanding designs tailored for elderly and diabetic patients.

### Microprocessor-Controlled Joints and Adaptive Hydraulics
At 39:01, Penn details the architecture of computerized prosthetics, highlighting microprocessor knees (such as the C-Leg) and powered bionic ankles (BiOM). He explains how onboard microcontrollers process accelerometer and gyroscope telemetry in real time to dynamically adjust hydraulic valving across swing and stance phases.

### Myoelectric Signal Filtering and Open-Source Collaboration
Concluding between 52:00 and 01:05:01, Penn reviews upper-limb myoelectric systems. Capturing and filtering faint electromyography (EMG) muscle signals through sweat and skin movement remains an immense challenge. He concludes by highlighting open-source maker initiatives developing accessible, 3D-printed prosthetic limbs for underserved communities.

### Bridging Forensic Science and Information Security
At 00:00, Najla Lindsay, a forensic scientist and information security professional, compares analytical methodologies between physical crime laboratories and digital cybersecurity operations at the Biohacking Village. Lindsay explores how foundational scientific principles enhance digital investigations.

### Maintaining Chain of Custody and Lab Integrity
At 09:11, Lindsay details procedural discipline inside clinical and forensic testing laboratories. She explains how laboratory personnel safeguard biological evidence, maintain rigorous chain of custody documentation, and resist social engineering attempts from individuals seeking unauthorized access to sensitive patient records.

### Methodological Parallels in Incident Response
At 17:24, the presentation maps physical forensic techniques to digital breach investigations. Lindsay demonstrates that hypothesis testing, sample preservation, contamination prevention, and structured evidence gathering apply identically whether analyzing physical crime scenes or parsing compromised memory dumps.

### Quality Assurance and Professional Accreditation Standards
At 25:44, the speaker reviews laboratory accreditation frameworks such as ISO 17025 and CLIA. She highlights how formal quality control protocols and blind proficiency testing reduce human error, advocating that digital forensics teams adopt similar rigorous validation standards.

### Cultivating Scientific Rigor in Cybersecurity
Concluding between 28:00 and 32:00, Lindsay encourages security analysts to approach threat hunting with a formal forensic mindset. By documenting investigative hypotheses, validating forensic tooling, and preserving digital evidence systematically, incident responders can produce audit-ready findings that withstand legal scrutiny.

talks.title: The L33T Shall Inherit the Cosmo
talks.teaser: Adapting human biological systems and DIY hacking methodologies for survival and autonomy in space environments.
talks.summary:
### Extreme Environmental Biology and Space Analog Habitats
At 00:00, biohacker and analog astronaut JJ Hastings delivers a keynote on human survival in extreme environments, exploring how biohacking and synthetic biology enable off-world human exploration.

### Whole-Genome Sequencing and Metabolic Self-Determination
At 06:00, Hastings recounts undergoing comprehensive whole-genome sequencing in 2016 through Project Demiurge. She explores how analyzing personal genomic data enables researchers to understand individualized physiological resilience, radiation sensitivity, and metabolic traits.

### The Architecture of Closed-Loop Analog Habitats
At 12:00, the speaker details life inside isolated space analog research facilities, such as the HI-SEAS habitat in Hawaii. She explores closed-loop life support engineering, detailing air filtration systems, water recycling loops, and onboard biological laboratories designed for planetary surface simulation missions.

### Sensory Deprivation and Psychological Resilience
At 18:02 and 24:01, Hastings shares the physical and psychological realities of prolonged isolation. Crews endure months of sensory deprivation—showering only once every two weeks, consuming dehydrated rations, and living under simulated planetary communication delays with zero outside contact.

### Microbiome Shifts and Interplanetary Evolution
Concluding at 30:01, Hastings presents research tracking human microbiome adaptations in sealed synthetic habitats. She argues that expanding humanity across the cosmos will require genetic engineering, closed-loop biomanufacturing, and synthetic biological enhancement to endure extraterrestrial environments.

talks.title: From Buffer Overflowing Genomics Tools to Securing
talks.teaser: Demonstrating a buffer overflow exploit in popular genomics alignment software (BWA) and steps to secure bioinformatics tools.
talks.summary:
### Software Vulnerabilities in Computational Biology Pipelines
At 00:00, Dr. Corey M. Hudson, computational biologist at Sandia National Laboratories, presents research exposing severe memory safety vulnerabilities across genomics software pipelines at the Biohacking Village. Dr. Hudson discusses the growing security risks in biological data processing.

### Fragile Genomics Software Architecture
At 08:56, Dr. Hudson examines the ecosystem of open-source bioinformatics tools, including sequence alignment utilities like BWA and SAMtools. He explains that these tools were historically developed by academic researchers focused on computational performance rather than defensive programming or secure memory management.

### Buffer Overflows via Crafted DNA Sequence Files
At 18:47, the presentation demonstrates how malformed biological data inputs compromise analytical software. By inserting overly long metadata headers or anomalous nucleotide sequences into FASTQ and FASTA files, researchers trigger classical buffer overflows and memory corruption within genomics parsing engines.

### Operational and Clinical Consequences in Biomanufacturing
At 27:43, Dr. Hudson outlines the catastrophic potential of targeted sequence exploitation. Maliciously manipulated genomic files can misdirect sequence alignment algorithms, causing false medical diagnoses or silently disrupting automated gene synthesis pipelines in biopharmaceutical manufacturing facilities.

### Hardening the Bioinformatics Toolchain
Concluding between 32:00 and 38:12, Dr. Hudson outlines defensive engineering priorities for the genomics community. He urges developers to transition toward memory-safe languages, implement robust input validation, and integrate automated fuzzing into bioinformatics software development.
